accuracy.evidence: I rechecked every value by hand. The turns are 90, 180 and 270 degrees. The sort set is 50 acute, two tilted 90s right, 125 obtuse, 25 acute and 230 reflex. The pairs are 60 against 40, 70 against 70 and 35 against 55. The missing angles are 180−130=50, 90−35=55 and 360−150−90=120. The isosceles figure has AB=AC and BD=DC, and AD is perpendicular to BC. Parameter corners stay valid: 180−a for a in 25..155 and 360−a−b is at least 100. The Year 3, 4 and 6 and CCSS 4.MD.5–7 wording matches the published texts.

misconceptions.evidence: The lab targets documented angle misconceptions from Clements and Battista and from Mitchelmore and White. These are: judging size by arm length or by how big the drawn arc is; seeing only horizontally based right angles as right angles (prototype orientation); reading tick marks as lengths or as parallel marks; taking the first letter of ∠XYZ as the vertex; and using 360° on a straight line. Each one appears as a prediction option, a sort item (tilted 90s), a marks distractor or a tagged challenge slip.

lab_distinct.evidence: This is a new flagangle lab that shares no code with the radian, unit circle, arc or symmetry labs. It has a rotating arm that snaps to 15° and draws the square at 90°, an orientation-varied angle sorter with four bins, a pair comparison with deliberately mismatched arm lengths, an isosceles triangle carrying the tick, arc and right-angle conventions, and missing-angle diagrams on a line, in a corner and round a point. It passed the 30% shingle gate.

lab_teaches.evidence: The order follows the curriculum. Angle as turn comes first (one, two and three right angles built on the same arm), then classification independent of orientation, then the idea that arm length is irrelevant, then reading conventions on a diagram, and finally using those conventions to compute unknowns. Each success line states the general rule, for example 'Subtract what you know from 180°, 90° or 360°'.

predictions.evidence: There are four locked predictions, each with the research-documented wrong answer offered. Two right angles make a straight line, with a full turn as the tempting option. Short wide arms beat long narrow arms, with the long arms as the tempting option. One tick on each of two sides means they are equal, with 1 cm and parallel as tempting options. Angles on a line sum to 180°, with 90° and 360° as tempting options. The step then has the learner act, and the reveal line reports whether the guess held.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six challenge questions carry nine tagged slips: acute versus obtuse, reflex versus obtuse, arm length, using 360° for a line, copying the given angle, taking the first letter or last letter as the vertex, a tick as 1 cm, a tick as parallel, and a tilted right angle. Each message names the slip and gives the correct reasoning with the question's numbers, e.g. 'A straight line is a half turn: 180 − 110 = 70'.

readability.evidence: The learner text uses short sentences and a body-turn opener (face the door, turn to the wall) for ages 8 to 12, with the exact terms acute, obtuse, reflex, vertex, right angle, tick and arc, each defined in place. The adult text quotes the programme-of-study statements and keeps sentences plain. Canvas headings are one line and every spoken message includes the degrees involved.

no_filler.evidence: It passed the filler scan and the 12% similarity gate against neighbouring geometry lessons (309 shapes, 474 symmetry, 133 radians and 112 the unit circle), which do not teach angle types or diagram conventions. Each learner paragraph adds one idea: turn, types, arm length, then marks and missing angles. The adult paragraphs cover the standards, the conventions, the named mistakes and the lab.

mobile.evidence: I checked screenshots at 360 px Android in light theme and iPhone 13 in dark theme, before and during Show me, for every step. The short-armed comparison angles were too small at first, so I lengthened them, gave both a fixed 18 px arc and checked again. The triangle labels, ticks and arcs stay legible, the four sort bins fit in one row, and the answer buttons wrap without clipping.

accessibility.evidence: The browser gate ran axe WCAG 2.1 AA in light and dark themes on desktop and iPhone 13, with no violations and no console errors. The arm drag has Turn 15° more and back buttons with aria labels, the sort bins have type buttons, the marks and missing-angle choices are real buttons, and the canvas aria-label is rewritten with each spoken message, including the current degrees and type.
